You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:
The test "testFloatValueForLargeNumeratorAndDenominator" creates very large BigInteger values as numerator and denominator, involving powers of 10 raised to 400 and 401 respectively. It then constructs a BigFraction from these large BigInteger values and asserts that the float representation of this fraction should be close to 5 with a tiny delta.

The current bug report indicates that the method BigFraction.doubleValue() fails for large numerators or denominators because the implementation simply calls numerator.doubleValue() divided by denominator.doubleValue(). The problem is that BigInteger.doubleValue() overflows to Double.NaN or otherwise behaves incorrectly for values much larger than Double.MAX_VALUE (approximately 1.8e308). Given that the numerator and denominator in the test have hundreds of digits, their doubleValue() calls will overflow or produce NaN, causing doubleValue() and floatValue() on BigFraction to produce incorrect results (NaN or similar), even when the actual fraction would be representable in double or float.

Inspecting the code snippets for BigFraction.floatValue() and BigFraction.doubleValue(), both methods do a direct division of numerator.floatValue()/denominator.floatValue() or numerator.doubleValue()/denominator.doubleValue(). Although comments in the code hint at considering range and shifting ("// Numerator and/or denominator must be out of range", "// Calculate how far to shift them to put them in range."), there is no actual implementation of such range adjustments. This indicates the methods are incomplete or not robust for extremely large values.

Hence the failure is the straightforward use of BigInteger.doubleValue()/floatValue() which does not handle overflow cases for very large numbers properly. The implemented method should include logic to scale down numerator and denominator appropriately before converting to double or float to avoid overflow yet preserve the fraction's value. The current implementation is incomplete and causes tests with very large numbers to fail or produce NaN.

The recent bug reports regarding unrelated optimization and simplex solver issues do not appear relevant to this arithmetic overflow bug with BigFraction.

Summary:
- BigFraction.doubleValue() and floatValue() just divide the double/float values of numerator and denominator
- BigInteger.doubleValue()/floatValue() overflows for large values > Double.MAX_VALUE
- Test uses 308+ digit numerator/denominator leading to overflow and NaN results
- Code comments hint at handling range scaling but code does not implement it
- A patch is needed to safely scale numerator and denominator before converting to double/float to prevent NaN on large BigFractions

This explains the test failure and the behavior described in the issue report.
